title: The Unexpected Vow Anew
premise: After a career-ending collapse on stage, cellist Wren Coldharbour retreats to the crumbling orchard he inherited from his grandmother, only to discover her deed names two other heirs: his first love, Ilsa Marchetti, and her half-brother Theo, a developer who wants to sell. As the three are forced to coexist through one growing season to satisfy the deed's strange residency clause, Wren and Ilsa confront the misunderstanding that ended them a decade ago, while Theo's corporate backers circle with an offer that could save each of them financially but destroy the orchard's community of workers who have become Wren's found family. When Theo betrays the deadline by filing to partition the land, Wren must choose between buying back his safe, broken life or staking everything—money, music, heart—on keeping the orchard whole. In the end, the trio finds a loophole in their grandmother's will, Theo walks away redeemed rather than ruined, and Wren performs again at the harvest festival, vowing anew to Ilsa under the old apple trees.
about_author: Felix Hartwell is the pen name of a former orchard hand turned novelist who writes love stories rooted in land, labor, and second chances. His work has been praised for its quiet emotional precision and its insistence that belonging is something we build, not inherit.

chapters.title: The Broken Bow
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A prologue-like opening replays the catastrophic final performance: mid-concerto, his hands fail him, and the hall goes silent as he walks off forever. The chapter establishes his shame, his severed ties, and the letter from a solicitor about an inheritance he barely remembers. Emotional beat: grief disguised as relief.

chapters.title: A Deed With Three Names
chapters.summary: Wren arrives at Coldharbour Orchard expecting solitude and finds a legal tangle: grandmother Edith's will grants the property jointly to him, Ilsa Marchetti, and a stranger named Theo Vance—contingent on all three residing there through harvest. Wren's POV; beat: dread sharpening into reluctant curiosity.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Packing Shed
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. She has been living secretly in the packing shed for weeks, also summoned by the will, and is furious to find Wren—the man who vanished on her ten years ago—listed beside her name. Their first confrontation crackles with old wounds. Beat: anger that keeps slipping into tenderness.

chapters.title: Terms of Residence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The solicitor explains the clause: ninety days of shared residence or the orchard reverts to county sale. Theo arrives unannounced with a surveyor and a smile, already measuring lots. Wren proposes they honor the season; Theo agrees for reasons of his own. Beat: uneasy truce.

chapters.title: Cider and Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The orchard's skeleton crew—foreman Del, young picker Marisol, ancient cook Bess—quietly adopt the newcomers, forcing Wren and Ilsa into shared meals and shared work. A near-kiss over a cider press is interrupted. Beat: warmth thawing frozen ground.

chapters.title: What the Hands Remember
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers Edith's old cello in the attic and cannot bring himself to open the case. Flashbacks reveal Ilsa was once his accompanist—and that his disappearance followed a betrayal he never explained. Beat: fear that music and love fail together.

chapters.title: Theo's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. We see his debts, his backers at Meridian Development, and his genuine surprise at liking the orchard's people. He begins drafting two futures: the sell-off plan and, guiltily, a restoration sketch. Beat: corruption beginning as convenience.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. A storm damages the west block; Wren works through the night beside the crew without complaint, earning grudging respect. Ilsa catches him playing the attic cello alone after midnight, badly, stubbornly. Beat: admiration complicating resentment.

chapters.title: The Letter She Never Sent
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He finds Edith's unsent letter revealing she knew why he left Ilsa—a protective lie involving Ilsa's father's bankruptcy—and that she engineered the three-name deed deliberately. Wren burns it unread halfway. Beat: the past pressing through floorboards.

chapters.title: Market Day
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The crew takes fruit to town; Meridian's representatives make a public offer that would set each heir up for life. Townsfolk split; Marisol's family faces losing their housing if the sale proceeds. Beat: money made visible as temptation.

chapters.title: Duet
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Forced to rehearse for the harvest festival by Bess's scheming, Wren and Ilsa play together for the first time in a decade. The old chemistry returns terrifyingly intact. They almost speak the truth of the past; instead they agree to try being friends. Beat: hope with teeth.

chapters.title: Rootstock
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Del teaches Theo grafting; Theo learns Edith saved his mother once, too—that he is more family than stranger. Meridian pressures him with a deadline and threats to expose his debts. Beat: loyalty pulling against leverage.

chapters.title: The Middle of It
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Wren finally tells Ilsa the truth: he left because her father begged him to, trading his future to shield hers from scandal. Ilsa is shattered—not by the lie but by the decade lost to it. They reconcile at dawn among the trees. Beat: catharsis.

chapters.title: Paperwork
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Happiness is interrupted: Theo files a partition petition, splitting the deed before the ninety days complete, which voids the residency clause and triggers sale. Wren realizes Theo's signature was the trap all along. Beat: betrayal landing like a dropped instrument.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. The crew rallies; Marisol reveals Meridian falsified environmental surveys. Ilsa organizes the workers, the town, and a legal challenge, discovering she has become the leader she never believed she was. Beat: found family becoming a fighting force.

chapters.title: The Empty Case
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finally opens the cello case and finds inside Edith's codicil: if any heir acts against the others' interest before harvest, their share passes to 'those who keep the trees.' Proof exists—but using it destroys Theo entirely. Beat: power offered as a moral test.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren and Ilsa confront Theo at the boundary stakes. Instead of ruining him, Wren offers him a way out: withdraw the petition, testify about Meridian's fraud, and come home. Theo, hollowed out, must choose. Beat: mercy as strength.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo testifies, torching his career and his backers, then picks apples beside the crew until his hands bleed and his shoulders finally loosen. The ninety days complete at midnight. Beat: redemption earned in labor, not words.

chapters.title: Meridian Descends
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Furious, Meridian escalates: a hostile bid, a court injunction attempt, intimidation of pickers. The community holds the line at a packed hearing where Del, Marisol, and even Theo speak. Beat: climax of external conflict.

chapters.title: The Vow Anew
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At the harvest festival, with the orchard's fate still hanging, Wren performs publicly for the first time since his collapse—shaking hands, full heart—and mid-piece asks Ilsa to marry him, promising to risk everything rather than lend pieces. She says yes before he finishes. Beat: romantic climax fused with artistic rebirth.

chapters.title: The Codicil Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Isla's POV. The judge honors Edith's codicil: the orchard passes to the three heirs and the crew collectively as a working trust. Theo, forgiven, becomes its business steward. The community celebrates under lanterns in the rows. Beat: belonging formalized as legacy.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Light
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue tone. One year later: the trust thrives, a small concert series runs in the barn, and Wren teaches local kids cello. On the morning of his wedding, he walks the orchard, thanks his grandmother aloud, and goes toward the music. Beat: peace earned, love kept in present tense.
